lead: The morning after Alphabet's record $500 billion wipeout, the details look more nuanced than the headline - revenue up 25%, cash flow negative for only the second time ever. Jassy tells investors outside shopping agents are 'still not great' while Alexa for shopping quietly posts 570% interaction growth. An open-weight model learns to exploit the browser patch gap for $1,000 a version, and the Show HN crowd compiles transformers into DOOM and web apps into Lean proofs.

sections.title: The reckoning, continued
sections.intro: Overnight coverage of Alphabet's record half-trillion wipeout, and what the same week says about Microsoft and Amazon.

sections.title: The consumer flank
sections.intro: Jassy waves off outside shopping agents while Alexa's own numbers do the talking, and Meta soft-launches an AI stylist in Southeast Asia.

sections.title: Deals and dollars
sections.intro: A $3 billion raise for Vera Rubin systems in India, Nvidia guaranteeing billions in data-center debt for an Anthropic facility, and API credits become the subscription bundle wars' latest salvo.

sections.title: The patch gap, weaponized
sections.intro: An open-weight model turns published-but-unshipped Firefox fixes into working exploits for about $1,000 a version.

sections.title: Games as compute
sections.intro: A transformer compiled into DOOM maps and verified against NumPy, and agent swarms loose in Minecraft and Mindustry.

sections.title: Proofs in production
sections.intro: Lasm compiles Lean 4 to WebAssembly so the web app you deploy is the one you proved.

sections.title: The harness diaries
sections.intro: Claude Duet wins over a skeptical reviewer with speed and channels, while HN debates whether Opus 5.5 got dumber overnight (the benchmark says no).

sections.title: Adoption notes
sections.intro: Proton, the privacy company, goes all in on AI.

sections.title: A bad day for trust
sections.intro: A trojanized Claude Code extension on the Cursor marketplace plants an SSH backdoor, a China-linked campaign runs 200 intrusions in 11 days with AI tooling, and the Linux TCP stack gets its own CVE.

sections.title: The economics seminar
sections.intro: A formal model of why the individual agent is the wrong economic unit: organizations, not people, are what AI has to outproduce.

sections.title: The conference circuit
sections.intro: AIE CODE takes shape: a thousand agentic engineers, three themes, and Bun's Rust rewrite on the marquee.

sections.title: Trust and antitrust
sections.intro: Regulators and campaign-money watchers close in: the UK CMA probes Meta's content terms, and FEC filings show the AI PAC money surprisingly favoring the pro-regulation side.

sections.title: The memory cycle turns
sections.intro: AI demand for memory is now visible on the income statement: CXMT swings to a big profit while Kioxia's blockbuster quarter comes with a cooler forecast.

sections.title: New models on every axis
sections.intro: Mistral releases the weights of its trillion-parameter flagship, Fish Audio and Pika push open weights in voice and video, and Figma trains a model fluent in its own editor.

sections.title: The interview circuit
sections.intro: Sam Altman argues against a single superintelligence over a pint, Neal Stephenson weighs what comes next, and Sharp Tech goes video with Anthropic's S-1 on the agenda.

sections.title: Rules for the machines
sections.intro: Two model specs surface at once: OpenAI reorganizes its Model Spec around five core values, and a leak reveals the charter Meta wrote for Muse.

sections.title: Plumbing for the agent economy
sections.intro: Natural lets agents choose their own payment rail at runtime - ACH, wire or realtime - with the operator's limits still in force.

sections.title: Research notes
sections.intro: An escape-room primer explains why RL environments are the currency of post-training, and an eight-agent experiment shows swarm leadership emerging from model choice and prompt order.
